description: 100 newly authored SL chemistry MCQs. Each row contains prompt, correct option, three distractors, explanation, inspiration paper, inspiration source ID. References identify topic inspiration, not authorship or an original IB question.

S1.1: A sealed flask contains only neon gas and nitrogen gas. How should its contents be classified?
A homogeneous mixture of two elements
A pure compound
A heterogeneous mixture of two compounds
A single element
Neon and nitrogen are elements. The gases mix uniformly without becoming chemically bonded to one another.
Which observation most strongly supports the conclusion that a sample is a mixture rather than a pure compound?
Different batches can contain different proportions of its components.
It occupies a fixed volume.
It contains more than one type of atom.
It has a measurable mass.
Mixtures can have variable composition; a particular pure compound has a fixed ratio of its constituent elements.
A sample consists entirely of identical molecules, each containing one sulfur atom and two oxygen atoms. What is the sample?
A pure compound
A mixture of sulfur and oxygen
A pure element
A heterogeneous mixture
Every particle has the same fixed combination of different elements, so the sample is a pure compound.
Liquid bromine contains only Br₂ molecules. Which classification is correct?
An element, because all atoms have the same atomic number
A compound, because each molecule has two atoms
A mixture, because many molecules are present
A compound, because it is liquid
An element can exist as diatomic molecules. The number of atoms per molecule does not determine whether it is a compound.
A beaker contains liquid water with floating ice, and no other substances. How is this sample best described?
A pure substance present in two physical states
A mixture of two chemical compounds
A mixture of two elements
A new compound formed from ice and water
Both phases consist of H₂O. More than one physical state does not by itself make a sample a mixture.
Which statement distinguishes a compound from a mixture?
Separating a compound into its constituent elements requires chemical change.
A compound must contain atoms in a variable ratio.
A mixture must contain at least one liquid.
A mixture must have components visible to the naked eye.
A compound contains chemically bonded elements; the components of a mixture can be separated by physical methods.
A clear solution of sodium chloride is sampled from its top and bottom after thorough mixing. What should be expected?
Both samples have the same composition, provided no evaporation occurs.
The top sample contains only water.
The bottom sample contains only sodium chloride.
The two samples must have different chemical formulas for water.
A homogeneous mixture is uniform in composition on the scale of ordinary sampling.
A mixture contains insoluble sand and aqueous sodium chloride. Which sequence can recover dry sand and solid sodium chloride separately?
Filter, then evaporate water from the filtrate
Evaporate all the water, then filter the dry residue
Filter, then discard the filtrate
Distil the sand before dissolving the salt
Filtration separates sand from the salt solution. Evaporating the filtrate leaves the dissolved salt.
During filtration of a suspension, what is the filtrate?
The liquid, including dissolved substances, that passes through the filter
Only the insoluble solid retained on the filter
Only chemically pure solvent in every case
The filter paper and all material on it
Filtration removes particles of insoluble material; dissolved substances generally pass through with the solvent.
Why does filtering a sodium chloride solution through ordinary filter paper fail to produce pure water?
The dissolved ions pass through the filter with the water.
The filter converts sodium chloride into a gas.
Sodium chloride must first become an element.
Water molecules cannot pass through filter paper.
Ordinary filtration does not separate a dissolved solute from its solvent.
A student wants to recover pure water from a solution of a non-volatile salt. Which process is appropriate?
Simple distillation with collection of the condensate
Filtration alone
Evaporation with the vapour allowed to escape
Grinding the salt solution
Water vaporizes and can be condensed separately while the non-volatile salt remains in the flask.

A solid is very soluble in hot water but only slightly soluble in cold water. Which method is suitable for obtaining purified crystals from a crude sample, assuming the impurities remain dissolved on cooling?
Recrystallization from hot water
Filtering a cold solution without cooling it further
Collecting only the water vapour
Mixing the solid with more insoluble impurities
Dissolving in hot solvent and cooling allows the desired solid to crystallize while the specified impurities remain in solution.
Two miscible liquids have boiling points of 65 °C and 82 °C. What normally becomes enriched in the first fraction collected during fractional distillation?
The liquid with the lower boiling point
The liquid with the higher boiling point
Both liquids in exactly their initial proportions at all times
A new compound with boiling point 147 °C
The more volatile component contributes a larger proportion of the vapour and is enriched in the early distillate.
Dry ice changes directly from solid carbon dioxide into gas. What is this change called?
Sublimation
Condensation
Deposition
Freezing
Sublimation is the direct change from solid to gas.
Water droplets form on the outside of a cold glass when water vapour in the surrounding air changes state. Which change occurs?
Condensation
Sublimation
Melting
Deposition
Water changes from gas to liquid, which is condensation.
Which description applies to the particles in a liquid?
They remain close together but can move past one another.
They occupy widely separated fixed positions.
They remain at rest unless the liquid boils.
They have no attractive interactions with neighbouring particles.
Liquid particles are close together and mobile, allowing a liquid to flow while retaining a nearly fixed volume.
A pure solid is heated at constant pressure and melts at its melting point. Why can its temperature remain constant while energy is supplied?
Energy changes particle interactions rather than increasing average kinetic energy during melting.
All particles stop moving during melting.
The supplied energy is destroyed.
The solid must lose all of its mass.
During a phase change at constant temperature, the energy supplied does not increase the particles' average kinetic energy.
A laboratory is at 27 °C. What is its temperature in kelvin, to the nearest kelvin?
T/K = temperature/°C + 273.15, so 27 °C is 300.15 K, approximately 300 K.
A sample warms from 15 °C to 33 °C. What is its temperature increase in kelvin?
Kelvin and Celsius intervals have the same size: 33 − 15 = 18 °C corresponds to 18 K.
A gas is heated from 250 K to 500 K. What happens to the average kinetic energy of its particles?
It doubles.
It halves.
It remains unchanged.
It increases by a factor of four.
Average kinetic energy is proportional to absolute temperature; 500/250 = 2.
S1.2: A neutral atom has atomic number 17 and mass number 37. How many neutrons does it contain?
The neutron number is mass number minus atomic number: 37 − 17 = 20.
An ion has 13 protons, 14 neutrons and 10 electrons. What is its charge?
The charge is the number of protons minus the number of electrons: 13 − 10 = +3.
How many electrons are present in an oxide ion, O²⁻, if oxygen has atomic number 8?
The ion has two more electrons than the neutral atom: 8 + 2 = 10.
Which pair represents isotopes of the same element?
Atoms with 6 protons and respectively 6 and 8 neutrons
Atoms with respectively 6 and 8 protons, each with 6 neutrons
Atoms with respectively 6 and 7 protons, each with mass number 14
Atoms with 6 and 8 protons, each having a neutral charge
Isotopes have the same proton number and different neutron numbers.
Which change would convert an atom of one element into an atom of a different element?
Changing the number of protons in the nucleus
Removing one electron
Adding one electron
Changing only the number of neutrons
The proton number defines the element; changes in electrons form ions and changes in neutrons form isotopes.
An atom of calcium-44 has atomic number 20. What remains unchanged when it forms Ca²⁺?
Its numbers of protons and neutrons
Its number of electrons and its charge
Its charge and its proton number
Its electron number and neutron number
Ion formation changes the number of electrons, not the composition of the nucleus.
Which statement correctly compares a proton with an electron?
They have opposite charges of equal magnitude, but the proton has a much greater mass.
They have identical charges and identical masses.
The electron has a positive charge and the proton a negative charge.
They have opposite charges and approximately equal masses.
A proton has relative charge +1 and an electron −1; the electron's mass is very small relative to the proton's.
Why is most of an atom's mass concentrated in its nucleus?
The nucleus contains protons and neutrons, which are much more massive than electrons.
The nucleus contains all the atom's electrons.
Electrons have no electric charge.
The nucleus occupies most of the atom's volume.
Protons and neutrons account for almost all atomic mass, although the nucleus occupies a very small volume.
A neutral atom contains 35 electrons and 45 neutrons. What is its mass number?
A neutral atom has 35 protons, so its mass number is 35 + 45 = 80.
An ion with charge 2− contains 18 electrons and 18 neutrons. What is its atomic number?
A 2− ion has two more electrons than protons, so the proton number is 18 − 2 = 16.
A hypothetical element has isotopes of mass numbers 10 and 11, with abundances of 20% and 80%. Using the mass numbers as isotopic masses, what is its relative atomic mass?
The weighted mean is (10 × 20 + 11 × 80)/100 = 10.8.
An element has only two isotopes, with masses taken as 63 and 65. Its relative atomic mass is 63.4. What is the percentage abundance of the isotope of mass 65?
If x is the fraction of the heavier isotope, 63(1 − x) + 65x = 63.4; x = 0.20.
An element has isotopes of mass numbers 24, 25 and 26 with abundances of 50%, 20% and 30%. Taking these mass numbers as isotopic masses, what is its relative atomic mass?
Two samples of the same element have different relative atomic masses. Which explanation can account for this?
The samples contain different proportions of the element's isotopes.
Every atom in one sample has a different proton number from every atom in the other.
Relative atomic mass changes whenever a sample changes state.
All neutrons have been converted into electrons in one sample.
Changing isotopic abundances changes the weighted mean atomic mass without changing the identity of the element.
Which statement about neutral atoms of carbon-12 and carbon-14 is correct?
They have the same number of electrons and different numbers of neutrons.
They have different numbers of protons and the same number of neutrons.
They have different electron configurations because their mass numbers differ.
Carbon-14 has two more protons than carbon-12.
Both isotopes have six protons and six electrons; they have six and eight neutrons respectively.
A species has 9 protons, 10 neutrons and 10 electrons. Which description is correct?
A fluoride ion with mass number 19 and charge 1−
A neon atom with mass number 20
A fluorine atom with mass number 19 and no charge
A fluoride ion with mass number 10 and charge 1+
Nine protons identify fluorine, 9 + 10 = 19 gives the mass number, and the extra electron gives charge −1.
Atoms X and Y both have mass number 40. X has 18 protons and Y has 20 protons. Which statement is correct?
X and Y are different elements, and X has two more neutrons than Y.
X and Y must be isotopes of the same element.
X and Y have the same number of neutrons.
X has two fewer neutrons than Y.
Their neutron numbers are 22 and 20. Equal mass numbers do not imply the same element.
Which species has the same number of electrons as a neutral neon atom (atomic number 10)?
Mg²⁺, with magnesium atomic number 12
Na, with sodium atomic number 11
F, with fluorine atomic number 9
Al⁺, with aluminium atomic number 13
Mg²⁺ has 12 − 2 = 10 electrons. The other species have 11, 9 and 12 respectively.
An element has two naturally occurring isotopes with masses taken as 79 and 81. The isotope of mass 81 becomes more abundant in a sample. What happens to the sample's relative atomic mass?
It increases towards 81.
It decreases towards 79.
It remains exactly 80 regardless of abundance.
It becomes greater than 81.
Increasing the weight of the heavier isotope increases the mean, which remains between the two isotope masses.
In a nuclear symbol, which quantity is given by the upper-left number, A?
The total number of protons and neutrons
The total number of protons and electrons
The number of neutrons minus the number of protons
The charge of the ion
A is the mass number, also called the nucleon number; it excludes electrons.
S1.3: Phosphorus has atomic number 15. Which is its ground-state electron configuration?
1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p³
1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁵
1s²2s²2p⁶3s¹3p⁴
1s²2s²2p⁵3s²3p⁴
Fifteen electrons fill the lower-energy sublevels before giving 3s²3p³ in the outer main energy level.
Which is the electron configuration of Cl⁻, given that chlorine has atomic number 17?
[Ne]3s²3p⁶
[Ne]3s²3p⁵
[Ne]3s²3p⁴
[Ar]4s¹
The chloride ion has 18 electrons, one more than the neutral chlorine atom.
Cobalt has atomic number 27 and the neutral configuration [Ar]3d⁷4s². Which is the configuration of Co²⁺?
[Ar]3d⁷
[Ar]3d⁵4s²
[Ar]3d⁶4s¹
[Ar]3d⁷4s²
The two 4s electrons are removed when Co²⁺ forms.
Which is the ground-state electron configuration of copper, atomic number 29?
[Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹
[Ar]3d⁹4s²
[Ar]3d⁸4s²4p¹
[Ar]3d¹⁰4s²
Copper is an exception to the simplest filling pattern and has a filled 3d sublevel with one 4s electron.
A neutral atom has configuration [Ne]3s²3p¹. What is its atomic number?
The neon core accounts for 10 electrons, and 3s²3p¹ adds three more. A neutral atom therefore has 13 protons.
What is the maximum number of electrons in the third main energy level?
A main energy level can hold 2n² electrons; with n = 3, this is 18.
How many orbitals are present in a p sublevel?
A p sublevel contains three orbitals with different spatial orientations; each can hold two electrons.
What is the maximum number of electrons that a d sublevel can contain?
A d sublevel contains five orbitals, each capable of holding two electrons.
Which statement correctly distinguishes a p orbital from a p sublevel?
One p orbital holds at most two electrons, while a complete p sublevel holds at most six.
One p orbital holds six electrons, while a p sublevel holds two.
A p orbital consists of three main energy levels.
A p sublevel contains only one orbital.
The p sublevel contains three p orbitals, each with a two-electron capacity.
Two electrons occupy the same orbital. Which arrangement is allowed?
They have opposite spins.
They must have parallel spins.
One must have a positive charge.
They must belong to different main energy levels.
The Pauli exclusion principle requires the two electrons in one orbital to have opposite spins.
Three electrons occupy the three p orbitals of an isolated atom in its ground state. Which arrangement follows Hund's rule?
One electron in each orbital, with parallel spins
Two electrons in one orbital and one in another, leaving the third empty
All three electrons in one orbital
One electron in each orbital, with all three having different charges
Degenerate orbitals are occupied singly with parallel spins before electrons pair.
How many unpaired electrons are present in the 2p sublevel of a ground-state oxygen atom with configuration 1s²2s²2p⁴?
For p⁴, three orbitals first receive one electron each; the fourth pairs in one, leaving two unpaired electrons.
Which feature correctly describes an s atomic orbital?
Its probability distribution is spherically symmetric about the nucleus.
It consists of two directional lobes separated by the nucleus.
It is a fixed circular path followed by an electron.
It can hold six electrons with the same spin.
An s orbital is spherically symmetric. An orbital describes an electron probability distribution, not a fixed path.
What happens when an electron in an isolated hydrogen atom moves from n = 2 to n = 5?
The atom absorbs energy.
The atom emits a photon.
The nucleus loses three protons.
The electron becomes positively charged.
Moving to a higher energy level requires absorption of energy.
Which electron transition in hydrogen emits ultraviolet radiation by ending at the first main energy level?
n = 3 to n = 1
n = 1 to n = 3
n = 4 to n = 2
n = 5 to n = 3
Emission to n = 1 belongs to the ultraviolet region; the upward transition is absorption.
Which transition in hydrogen can produce a visible emission line?
n = 4 to n = 2
n = 2 to n = 4
n = 2 to n = 1
n = 4 to n = 3
Visible hydrogen emission lines arise from higher levels falling to n = 2.
Blue light and red light travel at the same speed in a vacuum. Which comparison is correct?
Blue light has a higher frequency and higher photon energy than red light.
Blue light has a lower frequency and lower photon energy than red light.
Blue light has a longer wavelength and higher frequency than red light.
Both have the same frequency because their speeds are equal.
Blue light has a shorter wavelength, hence a higher frequency and higher photon energy.
Why does a hydrogen discharge tube produce separate emission lines instead of every possible colour?
Only certain differences between electron energy levels are possible.
Hydrogen contains several different elements.
Electrons can have any energy but emit only by chance.
Every photon emitted by hydrogen must have the same energy.
Discrete allowed electron energies produce photons with specific energies when transitions occur.
As the main energy level n increases in hydrogen, how does the spacing between adjacent energy levels change?
The levels become closer together.
The levels become farther apart by a constant amount.
The levels remain equally spaced.
Every higher level has less energy than n = 1.
Hydrogen energy levels converge at higher energies, so adjacent levels become closer together.
An electron falls between two energy levels separated by a larger energy gap than in another transition. How does the emitted photon compare?
It has higher frequency and shorter wavelength.
It has lower frequency and longer wavelength.
It has the same frequency but greater speed in a vacuum.
It has lower energy and shorter wavelength.
A larger energy gap gives a higher-energy photon; frequency increases while wavelength decreases.
S2.1: Which formula results when Li⁺ and O²⁻ form an electrically neutral ionic compound?
Li₂O
LiO
LiO₂
Li₂O₂
Two Li⁺ ions are required to balance the charge of one O²⁻ ion.
What is the formula of the ionic compound formed from Al³⁺ and O²⁻?
Al₂O₃
Al₃O₂
AlO
AlO₃
Two aluminium ions provide +6 and three oxide ions provide −6.
What is the formula of magnesium hydroxide?
Mg(OH)₂
MgOH
Mg₂OH
Mg₂(OH)₃
Mg²⁺ requires two hydroxide ions, each with charge −1.
Which is the formula of calcium nitrate?
Ca(NO₃)₂
CaNO₃
Ca₂NO₃
Ca(NO₂)₂
Calcium is Ca²⁺ and nitrate is NO₃⁻, so two nitrate ions are needed.
What is the formula of ammonium sulfate?
(NH₄)₂SO₄
NH₄SO₄
(NH₃)₂SO₄
NH₄(SO₄)₂
Two NH₄⁺ ions balance one SO₄²⁻ ion.
Which name correctly describes Cu₂O?
Copper(I) oxide
Copper(II) oxide
Copper(I) dioxide
Copper(II) peroxide
The oxide ion has charge −2, so each of the two copper ions must have charge +1.
What is the formula of iron(III) chloride?
FeCl₃
Fe₃Cl
FeCl₂
Fe₂Cl₃
Iron(III) is Fe³⁺; three chloride ions are needed per iron ion.
Which is the correct name for NaHCO₃?
Sodium hydrogencarbonate
Sodium carbonate
Sodium hydroxide
Sodium hydrogen sulfite
The anion HCO₃⁻ is hydrogencarbonate; carbonate is CO₃²⁻.
A main-group atom has outer-shell configuration 3s²3p⁵. Which ion does it normally form to achieve a noble-gas configuration?
A 1− ion by gaining one electron
A 1+ ion by losing one electron
A 5+ ion by losing five protons
A 2− ion by gaining two neutrons
Seven outer-shell electrons become eight when one electron is gained, giving charge −1.
Why does losing two electrons from a neutral magnesium atom produce a positive ion?
The ion has two more protons than electrons.
The ion has gained two protons.
The two lost electrons had positive charge.
The ion has lost two neutrons.
The nucleus is unchanged; removing negatively charged electrons leaves a net positive charge.
Which statement describes the ionic bond in sodium fluoride?
Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions
Attraction between neutral molecules only
Sharing of a single pair of electrons between two neutral atoms
Attraction between positive ions and a sea of delocalized electrons
Ionic bonding is the electrostatic attraction between cations and anions.
Why does molten sodium chloride conduct electricity while solid sodium chloride does not conduct appreciably?
Its ions can move through the liquid but are fixed in the solid lattice.
It contains ions only after melting.
Melting converts all chloride ions into free electrons.
The solid has no charged particles.
Mobile ions transport charge in the melt; the solid contains ions but they cannot move through the lattice.
A substance has a high melting point, does not conduct electricity as a solid, and conducts when molten. Which structure best explains these observations?
An ionic lattice
Separate non-polar molecules
A metallic lattice
Separate atoms of a noble gas
The observations are characteristic of an ionic solid whose ions become mobile on melting.
What does the formula CaF₂ represent in a crystal of calcium fluoride?
A 1:2 ratio of calcium ions to fluoride ions in an extended lattice
Individual CaF₂ molecules held together by hydrogen bonds
A 2:1 ratio of calcium ions to fluoride ions
Two calcium atoms sharing one electron with one fluorine atom
An ionic formula expresses the simplest electrically neutral ratio of ions, not discrete molecules.
Two ionic solids have ions of the same charge but different ionic radii. Which change generally strengthens the electrostatic attraction?
Decreasing the distance between the ion centres
Increasing the distance between the ion centres
Removing all charges from the ions
Replacing attraction with repulsion
For fixed charges, electrostatic attraction increases as the separation decreases.

Two hypothetical ionic lattices have similar distances between neighbouring ions. Lattice X contains 1+ and 1− ions; lattice Y contains 2+ and 2− ions. Which has stronger attraction between neighbouring unlike ions?
Y, because the magnitudes of the ionic charges are larger
X, because its ions have smaller charge magnitudes
Both must have identical attractions
Neither, because unlike charges repel
At similar separations, larger ionic charge magnitudes give stronger electrostatic attraction.
Why do many ionic compounds have low volatility?
Substantial energy is needed to overcome strong attractions throughout the lattice.
Their particles have no mass.
They consist of weakly attracted gas molecules.
Their ions become uncharged whenever heated.
Strong lattice attractions make it difficult for particles to escape into the gas phase.
Which statement about ionic compounds is correct?
Their solubility in water varies; not all ionic compounds dissolve readily.
Every ionic compound is highly soluble in water.
All ionic compounds conduct electricity well as solids.
Every ionic compound consists of discrete two-ion molecules.
An ionic structure does not guarantee high water solubility; properties depend on the particular compound.
Which substance contains covalent bonds within a polyatomic ion and ionic attractions between ions?
NH₄Cl
Cl₂
HCl
CH₄
Ammonium chloride has covalent N–H bonds within NH₄⁺ and ionic attractions between NH₄⁺ and Cl⁻.
An ionic compound contains M³⁺ and sulfate ions, SO₄²⁻. What is its empirical formula?
M₂(SO₄)₃
M₃(SO₄)₂
MSO₄
M(SO₄)₃
Two M³⁺ ions and three sulfate ions give charges of +6 and −6.
S2.2: What holds the two hydrogen atoms together in an H₂ molecule?
Attraction between the shared electron pair and both positive nuclei
Repulsion between the two positive nuclei
Attraction between two negative hydrogen ions
Hydrogen bonding between the two atoms
A covalent bond involves a shared electron pair attracted to the positively charged nuclei of both atoms.
How many electrons are shared in the N≡N bond of nitrogen gas?
A triple bond contains three shared electron pairs, hence six bonding electrons.
For bonds between the same pair of elements, how does a triple bond generally compare with a single bond?
It is shorter and stronger.
It is longer and weaker.
It is shorter and weaker.
It has the same length and strength.
Greater bond order generally increases bond strength and decreases bond length for the same bonded elements.
In the usual Lewis formula O=C=O, how many lone pairs are present on each oxygen atom?
Each oxygen has two bonding pairs in its double bond and two lone pairs, completing an octet.
In the Lewis formula of hydrogen peroxide, H–O–O–H, how many lone pairs are present in the whole molecule?
Each oxygen forms two single bonds and has two lone pairs, giving four lone pairs in total.
Ammonia donates its nitrogen lone pair to H⁺ to form NH₄⁺. Where do both electrons in the newly formed bond originally come from?
The nitrogen atom of ammonia
One from nitrogen and one from H⁺
Both from H⁺
Neither atom; they are created during bond formation
In a coordination bond, both electrons of the shared pair originate from the donor atom.
A central atom has three bonding domains and no lone pairs. What molecular geometry does the VSEPR model predict?
Trigonal planar
Trigonal pyramidal
Tetrahedral
Bent
Three electron domains arrange in a plane approximately 120° apart; with no lone pairs, the molecular geometry is trigonal planar.
A central atom has two bonding domains and two lone pairs. What are its electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry, respectively?
Tetrahedral and bent
Linear and linear
Trigonal planar and bent
Tetrahedral and trigonal pyramidal
Four electron domains give tetrahedral electron-domain geometry; the two bonded atoms form a bent molecular shape.
Why is the H–O–H angle in water smaller than the ideal tetrahedral angle?
Lone pairs repel bonding domains more strongly than bonding domains repel one another.
Oxygen has no valence electrons.
The two hydrogen nuclei attract each other more strongly than they attract electrons.
The O–H bonds are ionic, so VSEPR cannot apply.
Water has two lone pairs whose stronger repulsion compresses the angle between its bonding domains.
Electronegativities are H = 2.2, C = 2.6, N = 3.0 and O = 3.4. Which of these bonds is most polar?
O–H
C–H
N–H
C–N
The electronegativity differences are 1.2, 0.4, 0.8 and 0.4 respectively; O–H has the largest difference.
Why is a carbon dioxide molecule non-polar even though each C=O bond is polar?
The equal bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel in its linear geometry.
Carbon and oxygen have identical electronegativities.
A double bond cannot be polar.
The molecule contains mobile ions that neutralize its dipole.
Molecular polarity depends on the vector sum of bond dipoles; the two equal dipoles cancel in linear CO₂.
Which molecule has a net dipole moment?
CH₃Cl
CO₂
BF₃
CCl₄
The bond dipoles in CH₃Cl do not cancel. The other listed molecules have symmetric geometries that cancel their bond dipoles.
Which intermolecular force is present between molecules of every molecular substance, including non-polar substances?
London dispersion forces
Hydrogen bonding
Permanent dipole–dipole attraction
Ionic bonding
Fluctuations in electron distributions create instantaneous and induced dipoles, giving London forces in all molecular substances.
Which pure liquid can form hydrogen bonds between its own molecules?
CH₃CH₂OH
CH₃OCH₃
CH₃CH₃
CH₃Cl
Ethanol has an O–H group and oxygen lone pairs. The other substances lack a hydrogen bonded directly to N, O or F.
Ethanol and dimethyl ether have the same molecular formula, C₂H₆O. Why does ethanol have the higher boiling point?
Ethanol molecules can hydrogen-bond to one another, whereas dimethyl ether molecules cannot do so with one another.
Ethanol has ionic bonds while dimethyl ether has covalent bonds.
Dimethyl ether has no intermolecular attractions at all.
Ethanol has twice as many electrons in each molecule.
The O–H group permits intermolecular hydrogen bonding in ethanol; dimethyl ether has no suitable donor hydrogen.
Which alcohol is expected to be the most soluble in water?
Methanol, CH₃OH
Hexan-1-ol, C₆H₁₃OH
Octan-1-ol, C₈H₁₇OH
Decan-1-ol, C₁₀H₂₁OH
All have an –OH group, but methanol has the smallest non-polar hydrocarbon part and is most compatible with water.
Why does diamond have a very high melting temperature?
Strong covalent bonds extend throughout its three-dimensional network.
It consists of separate molecules joined only by London forces.
It is held together by hydrogen bonds between carbon atoms.
It contains a lattice of C⁴⁺ and C⁴⁻ ions.
Changing the solid network requires overcoming strong covalent bonding, rather than only weak intermolecular forces.
Why can graphite conduct electricity along its layers?
Some electrons are delocalized and can move through the layers.
Carbon nuclei move freely between electrodes.
Graphite contains free chloride ions.
All carbon–carbon bonds disappear at room temperature.
Graphite has mobile delocalized electrons that can transport charge along its layers.
Which comparison of silicon dioxide and sulfur dioxide is correct?
Solid SiO₂ has a covalent network, whereas SO₂ consists of separate molecules.
Both substances consist of identical giant ionic lattices.
SiO₂ consists of individual molecules, whereas SO₂ has a giant covalent network.
Neither substance contains covalent bonds.
Silicon dioxide is an extended covalent network; sulfur dioxide is a molecular substance with intermolecular attractions.
A non-polar molecule approaches a polar molecule. Which interaction can result when the polar molecule distorts the other's electron distribution?
Dipole-induced dipole attraction
Formation of an ionic lattice in every case
A coordination bond in every case
Hydrogen bonding even when neither molecule contains hydrogen
A permanent dipole can induce a dipole in a neighbouring non-polar molecule, producing an attractive interaction.
